Types of restaurant SMS marketing campaigns Restaurants can send one-time campaigns for immediate opportunities or automated campaigns triggered by guest behavior. The right format depends on your restaurant’s goal and when the message will be useful. Campaign format Best suited for Examples One-time campaign A particular date, offer, event, location, or immediate business need Limited-time promotions, slow-day offers, events, holiday menus, or reservation availability Automated campaign Ongoing communication triggered by guest activity Welcome, We Miss You, Big Spender, Repeat Guest, or Post-Purchase messages One-time SMS campaigns A one-time campaign works best when a restaurant has something timely to communicate. The message is created and scheduled for a specific audience rather than triggered automatically by individual guest behavior. Restaurants can use one-time campaigns to: Promote a limited-time menu item. Increase orders during a slower daypart. Announce an event or holiday menu. Fill last-minute reservation availability. Share a subscriber-only offer. Direct guests to online ordering . Promote an offer at a particular restaurant location. Real-time promotions can attract attention while guests are deciding where to eat. According to the National Restaurant Association , 86% of full-service restaurant customers said they would likely pay attention to and use a real-time promotion from a restaurant in their area. Restaurants can also coordinate SMS with other marketing channels. During the 2022 NBA Finals, Chipotle displayed text-to-claim keywords in television ads for buy-one-get-one-free offers. The first offer was exhausted in two minutes, while offers during Games 3 and 4 were claimed in under 30 seconds, according to Marketing Dive . Chipotle executive Tressie Lieberman said the campaign “taps into the consumer behavior of watching sports alongside a second screen.” Automated SMS campaigns Automated campaigns send messages when a guest meets a specified signup, visit, purchase, or spending condition. Once the campaign is active, the restaurant doesn’t need to schedule each message individually. For example, Toast supports several automated SMS campaign types: Welcome: Send an introductory message or offer when someone joins the SMS list. We Miss You: Contact a guest after a selected number of days without a visit. Big Spender: Recognize guests who meet a chosen spending threshold. Repeat Guest: Thank or reward guests after they reach a selected visit count. Post-Purchase: Follow up one day after a guest’s order. Connecting automated messages with a restaurant loyalty program can help operators recognize returning guests and provide relevant reasons to visit again. Jason Wolbransky, general manager of Dog & Bull Taphouse and Kitchen, described the benefit of keeping these campaigns running in the background: “The automated campaigns are great, too—I turn them on, and they run in the background. On average we’ve been able to generate $34 in sales per automated text sent, which can add up quickly as I grow my subscriber list.”** Restaurant SMS marketing best practices Effective SMS marketing is relevant, easy to act on, and respectful of the guest’s permission and attention. These practices can help restaurants build a healthier subscriber list and produce stronger campaigns. 1. Grow the subscriber list through existing touchpoints Guests need a clear and convenient way to join the SMS list. Restaurants can promote enrollment through: Email campaigns Social media Restaurant signage QR codes Text to Join Online ordering Loyalty enrollment POS text receipts Regardless of the signup channel, restaurants should clearly explain what subscribers are agreeing to receive. 2. Keep each message concise and focused An effective restaurant text should communicate its value quickly. Guests should immediately understand who sent the message, why it matters, and what they can do next. Identify the restaurant: Use a recognizable sender name. Give the text one purpose: Focus on one offer, event, or announcement. Lead with the value: Put the reason to act near the beginning. Use a consistent voice: Write in a style guests will recognize from the restaurant. Account for message length: Emojis, special characters, and additional segments may affect text usage. Trying to promote several unrelated offers in one message can weaken the call to action. Save the wider update for email and use SMS to highlight the most timely opportunity. 3. Create a direct path to the next action Every promotional text should make the next step clear. Depending on the campaign, that could mean including a promo code or link to: Online ordering Reservations Loyalty enrollment Gift cards An event page The restaurant’s website For example, a restaurant promoting last-minute availability can direct subscribers to Toast Tables , where they can join a waitlist or make a reservation. Connecting the message directly to the intended action reduces the number of steps between receiving the text and responding to it. 4. Respect timing and message frequency Send texts when the information is useful and the restaurant can handle the response. A lunch offer should arrive before guests have made lunch plans, while an event announcement needs enough lead time for them to act. Restaurants should also: Follow applicable quiet-hour requirements. Avoid texting so frequently that guests tune out or unsubscribe. Coordinate SMS with email and social media campaigns. Make it easy for subscribers to opt out. There is no universal sending frequency that fits every restaurant. Monitor engagement and unsubscribe activity to determine what works for the audience. 5. Protect campaign deliverability A campaign cannot drive results if carriers do not deliver it. Restaurants should maintain accurate subscriber data and watch for patterns that may cause filtering. Remove invalid phone numbers. Honor opt-out requests. Monitor failed deliveries and unsubscribe rates. Avoid misleading language or excessive punctuation. Send messages only to guests who provided the required consent. High unsubscribe rates can signal that messages are too frequent, poorly timed, or insufficiently relevant. 6. Measure business results Message deliveries and link clicks indicate whether guests received and interacted with a campaign, but restaurants should also evaluate what happened afterward. To get a full picture of your ROI , review metrics such as: Messages delivered Link clicks Unsubscribes Orders Estimated sales Performance by campaign type The most important metric depends on the campaign’s original goal. A limited-time ordering promotion should be evaluated based on orders and sales, while a subscriber-growth campaign should focus on qualified opt-ins.
